Team Git Workflow
Standard git workflow for team projects. Applies any time Claude is helping with git operations — commits, branches, merges, PRs — on a team codebase.
Branches
    • main — the stable, always-up-to-date version of the code. Nothing goes here until it's reviewed and agreed on.
    • Feature branches — one per feature (e.g. a new page, a new endpoint). Branch off main.
        ◦ Examples: applicant-profile-page, cv-upload, nqf-dropdown
        ◦ Keep names short, lowercase, hyphenated.
Committing
Always ask before committing. Never run git commit (or git push) without first showing the proposed commit message(s) and getting an explicit go-ahead. This applies even if the work is clearly finished.
One commit per independent unit of work. A unit of work is a single feature, a single bug fix, a single refactor, etc. — things that don't depend on each other. If a change touches two unrelated things, split it into two commits (and ask about each separately if needed). Don't bundle "add CV upload" and "fix typo in nav" into one commit.
Scoped commits, simple humanized tags. Format:
tag: short plain-English description
    • Tag is one lowercase word, no parentheses/scopes (skip feat(auth): style — keep it simple)
    • Common tags: feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, style, test
    • Description is imperative, no trailing period: feat: add CV upload button, not feat: Added CV upload button.
    • No walls of text in the subject line — if more detail is needed, put it in the commit body, not the tag line Examples:
    • feat: add NQF qualification dropdown
    • fix: correct SAQA lookup validation
    • refactor: simplify applicant form state
    • chore: bump supabase client version
Checking for sensitive info before committing
Before proposing any commit, check the staged changes for secrets or sensitive data — don't just trust .gitignore. Look for things like:
    • API keys, tokens, or credentials (e.g. Supabase service role keys, JWT secrets)
    • .env files or hardcoded connection strings/passwords
    • Private keys or certificates (.pem, .key, etc.)
    • Any personal data that shouldn't be in the repo Practically:
    1. Run git diff --staged (or check git status for files about to be added) and scan it yourself before writing the commit message.
    2. If something sensitive shows up, stop and flag it — don't commit it, and suggest moving it to a .env file (added to .gitignore) or an untracked config file instead.
    3. If a secret has already been committed in an earlier commit, flag that separately — removing it from the latest commit isn't enough, it's still in git history and the key should be rotated.
Merging back to main
Only merge a feature branch into main once all team members have reviewed the code and agree it's good and finished. Before merging:
    1. Confirm the branch has actually been reviewed (don't assume — ask the user if the team has signed off).
    2. If there's no confirmation that everyone agrees, don't merge — flag it and suggest opening/continuing a PR for review instead.
Quick workflow summary
    1. Branch off main for the feature.
    2. Do the work.
    3. When a self-contained unit of work is done, check the staged changes for secrets/sensitive info, then propose a commit message using the tag format above and ask before committing.
    4. Push the feature branch.
    5. Open for team review (PR or equivalent).
    6. Merge to main only once everyone has reviewed and agreed it's finished.

Coding Conventions
Apply these conventions when writing or reviewing code.
Design
    • Follow SOLID object-oriented design principles where applicable: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
Naming
    • Variables are nouns. Prefer elapsed_time_in_days = 0 over d = 0.
    • Functions are verbs. Prefer update_item_price() over item_updater().
    • Avoid disinformation. Don't name something in a way that misrepresents what it is — e.g. don't call a list an "array", don't name a variable accountList if it's actually a Map.
    • Include units of measurement in variable names when the variable measures something. Prefer time_in_milliseconds over time.
Functions
    • Keep functions small. Each function should do one thing, contain few lines, and prefer a single level of indentation. Treat this as a strong preference, not a hard limit — don't over-extract trivial one-line helpers just to satisfy the rule.
General
    • Avoid magic numbers and strings. Use named constants instead of unexplained literals.
    • Use consistent casing per language convention — e.g. snake_case for Python, camelCase for JavaScript/Java — matching the idiomatic style of the language in use.
Documentation
    • Document code as it's written, not after. Add docstrings/comments in the same pass as writing the function, not as a cleanup step later.
    • Be descriptive about how functions work — explain what the function does, its parameters, return value, and any non-obvious behavior or edge cases, not just a one-line restatement of the function name.
CRUD Methodology
    • Adhere to CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) methodology when designing functions and data-handling code. Each function should map clearly to one of these operations rather than mixing several — e.g. keep create_user(), get_user(), update_user(), and delete_user() as separate functions instead of one function that both creates and updates records.

I scanned the full diff — no secrets, credentials or .env changes; the only strings that look configuration-shaped are the REGULAR/PLAYOFFS enum values.
Two things worth flagging before you decide:
The doc's riskiest assumption held up, and one detail was wrong. I verified live against stats.nba.com rather than trusting the doc. "PlayIn" and "Playoffs" are correct for nba_api 1.11.4, and Finals detection via the round digit is sound — the 2025-26 playoff ids split 48/21/11/5 across rounds 1–4, exactly a real bracket, with the five round-4 games resolving to SAS vs. NYK in June 2026. But play-in games carry their own 005 id prefix, not the 004 the doc assumed, so they never need round parsing at all. The doc's suggested PlayoffSeries cross-check endpoint doesn't exist under that name in this version (it's CommonPlayoffSeries) — I didn't need it, and noted it as the fallback.
One deliberate departure from the plan. I also added seasonType to GET /v1/players/compare, which section 6 didn't list. Comparing two players from inside a playoffs view would otherwise silently answer a regular-season question. Say the word if you'd rather I drop it.

All six steps of the plan are done. Seven commits on postseason-view, working tree clean, everything green:
Suite	Result
API (apps/api)	102 passed (was 79)
Web (apps/web)	154 passed (was 131)
Ingestion (apps/ingestion)	18 passed (new)
Typecheck + lint	Clean on both apps

What shipped, against the plan's four requirements:
    1. Ingestion — a postseason phase pulling play-in, playoffs and Finals, classified from game ids.
    2. Strict isolation — enforced by the query on both sides: where: { game: { seasonType } } server-side, separate cache keys client-side. Tested with a distinct points-per-game per segment so any bleed changes a number rather than hiding behind an equal average.
    3. Participation filter — ?seasonType=PLAYOFFS&participated=true, wired into the players list for postseason segments only.
    4. Performance change view — GET /v1/players/:id/stats/splits behind a "Regular season vs. postseason" table with signed deltas.
On the pitfalls you flagged:
The play-in filtering worked out better than the doc expected — I verified live rather than trusting it. "PlayIn"/"Playoffs" are correct for nba_api 1.11.4, and Finals detection via the round digit holds (the 2025-26 playoff ids split 48/21/11/5 across rounds 1–4, a real bracket, with round 4 resolving to SAS vs. NYK in June 2026). But play-in games carry their own 005 id prefix, so they never need round parsing at all — simpler and more robust than the doc's plan. The doc's suggested PlayoffSeries cross-check doesn't exist under that name in this version (it's CommonPlayoffSeries); I didn't need it and noted it as the fallback. The classifier falls back to regular season for an unreadable id, so a bad id can never silently corrupt a postseason view.
Two things worth your attention before review:
    • The contamination guard is the load-bearing commit. fix: keep postseason games out of prediction and optimizer models is what stops this feature being a regression to Elo, Four Factors, the optimizer and predicted scorers. Postseason games are a player's most recent games, so under recency weighting they'd carry the heaviest weight of all. That's tested with a target game where a leak could not produce the expected 20.0.
    • Two scope departures, both small and easy to revert: I added seasonType to GET /v1/players/compare (section 6 didn't list it — without it, comparing from inside a playoffs view silently answers a regular-season question), and I clear the local "what if" stat edits on segment change for the same isolation reason.
Per the team workflow the branch is not pushed and not merged — that needs team review first. Say the word and I'll push postseason-view and open a PR.

I ran the whole path myself first, so everything below is verified rather than guessed.
1. Read the code (~30 min)
Review in commit order — each builds on the last, and the messages carry the reasoning:
git log --oneline main..postseason-view      # 7 commits
git show 9508ade                              # schema + migration
git show f664636                              # ← the important one
git diff main..postseason-view                # everything (2039 insertions)
Spend your review budget on f664636 (the model guard). The schema and UI commits are mechanical; that one is the difference between this being a new feature and a silent regression to Elo, Four Factors, the optimizer and predicted scorers. Ask specifically: is there any other query that aggregates PlayerGameStat or Game without a season filter? I audited for this, but it's the thing worth a second pair of eyes.
The second-best question to bring: should the play-in be grouped with the playoffs? The plan left it a distinct segment, and merging them later in the UI is easy. That's a product call the team hasn't actually made.
2. Run the automated tests (~3 min)
npm run db:up:test          # disposable test DB, port 55433
npm test                    # API (102) + Web (154)

cd apps/ingestion && ./.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pytest test_games.py -q   # 18
The tests worth reading rather than just running:
    • apps/api/test/players.e2e-spec.ts — the isolation guarantee. Each segment gets a distinct points-per-game, so a bleed changes a number instead of hiding behind an equal average.
    • apps/api/test/games.e2e-spec.ts → "ignores postseason games when predicting scorers".
    • apps/ingestion/test_games.py — every id is a real 2025-26 id pulled live, including the five actual Finals games.
3. Click through it (~10 min)
Your dev DB was seed data (4 teams / 12 games), so re-seeding is safe — I already did both steps:
npm run db:up
cd apps/api && npx prisma migrate deploy && npm run prisma:seed
npm run api:dev            # terminal 1
npm run web:dev            # terminal 2
The seeded postseason is 12 regular · 2 play-in · 10 playoff · 4 Finals games. Things to try:
Where	What to check
/players/<id>?segment=finals	Reload it — the segment survives, so the link is shareable
A Lakers player → Play-In	Should say "did not play in the Play-In", not show zeros as bad play
Any player, bottom of profile	Regular-vs-postseason table with signed deltas
/players?segment=finals	Only LAL and BOS players (6, down from 14)
/predictions?segment=playoffs	Explains models are regular-season only, rather than a wall of "No prediction yet"
Edit a stat, then switch segment	The edit clears — a regular-season override can't linger over Finals numbers

The one manual check the tests can't make: open a player's Playoffs view and confirm the numbers differ from their Regular view. If they're ever identical, that's the bug worth catching.
4. What I could not verify
I did not run the real ingestion — that needs the ~25–35 minute residential-network run, and production data is loaded by hand rather than through a deploy. I verified the endpoints and id classification live against stats.nba.com, and the classifier against real 2025-26 ids, but the end-to-end postseason ingest against a live database is untested. That's the main gap to close before this reaches production data — and it's re-runnable and idempotent, so it can be run on its own without redoing the regular season.

Here's how each part actually works.
The migration: you don't run it — merging does
Verified in render.yaml:
branch: main
startCommand: npx prisma migrate deploy && npm start
Prod applies pending migrations automatically on every API boot, from main. That's exactly the fix in commit dbf7bbd, after the player_bio_fields migration shipped late and 500'd every player query. So the sequence is:
    1. Team reviews and approves postseason-view
    2. Merge to main
    3. Render redeploys → migrate deploy adds seasonType / playoffRound → API starts
If the migration fails, the service refuses to start rather than serving code against a schema missing columns it queries. That's deliberate, and it's the behaviour you want.
Don't apply it by hand. Running migrate deploy against prod yourself before merging would put the schema ahead of the deployed code. That direction is harmless here (new columns with defaults, nothing reads them yet), but it desyncs _prisma_migrations from what's on main and you lose the guarantee that the running code matches the schema. Let the deploy do it.
One ordering note: the web app deploys separately to Cloudflare Pages. If it lands before the API, degradation is graceful — an old API ignores ?seasonType= and returns regular season, and the profile page shows "Could not load postseason splits" rather than breaking. Deploying the API first avoids even that.
The ingestion: use the new single-phase script
Answering this exposed a gap in what I'd delivered, so I fixed it. ingest.py runs every phase in sequence with no way to skip — against prod, which already has teams, rosters and bios, that means re-fetching ~500 player bios to add ~90 games. ~30 minutes of API calls to do ~5 minutes of work.
I added apps/ingestion/ingest_postseason.py, following the same standalone-phase pattern as the existing backfill_player_bios.py. It reads the team/player id maps straight from the database instead of re-fetching them:
cd apps/ingestion
# point DATABASE_URL at the Render Postgres — an external connection string
python ingest_postseason.py
I smoke-tested it end to end against live stats.nba.com short of the boxscore writes: DB reads fine, fetched 91 real games, classified as 6 play-in / 80 playoffs / 5 Finals.
Three things that matter for the prod run:
    • This has to run from your own machine, not a cloud host — stats.nba.com blocks cloud-provider IP ranges.
    • Use .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip rather than bare pip if you need to install into the venv — the new pytest line in requirements.txt is test-only and not needed for the ingest itself.
    • Never run npm run prisma:seed against prod. resetGameData() deletes every Game/GameEvent/PlayerGameStat row. It's the single most destructive thing in the repo and it's one typo away from the seed command you've been running locally.
Your existing regular-season rows need no cleanup — the migration defaults them to REGULAR, which is accurate, since they were all ingested with season_type_nullable="Regular Season".
Order matters: migration (via merge) first, then ingestion. The script writes seasonType, so the column has to exist. Run it before the merge and it fails on an unknown column.

ingest_postseason.py and the README section are on the branch but not committed. Suggested: feat: add a postseason-only ingestion script. Want me to commit it? It's genuinely part of this feature — without it, the prod path costs 30 minutes instead of 5.

Both .env files are gitignored and untracked, so pointing them at prod won't leak a connection string into a commit.
Steps
1. Get the External connection string from the Render dashboard (Postgres → External Database URL). The internal one only resolves inside Render. Append ?sslmode=require.
2. Back it up first — you're hand-writing to prod, and this makes the whole thing reversible:
docker run --rm postgres:16-alpine pg_dump "<PROD_URL>" > prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql
3. Verify your shell override actually points at prod before writing anything. apps/api/.env also defines DATABASE_URL; a shell variable should win, but check rather than trust it:
cd apps\api
$env:DATABASE_URL = "<PROD_URL>?sslmode=require"
npx prisma migrate status      # read-only
You want it to report 20260907101500_add_game_season_type as pending. If it says the DB is up to date, the override didn't take and you're looking at your local DB — stop and fix that first.
4. Apply the migration:
npx prisma migrate deploy
5. Check prod already has full rosters, since that decides which ingestion script to use:
docker run --rm postgres:16-alpine psql "<PROD_URL>" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM \"Team\";"
If that's 30, use the fast path — prod has the teams and bios already, so you only need the postseason:

cd ..\ingestion

(If it's 4, prod only has seed data and you'd want the full ingest.py instead.)
6. Run the branch locally against prod — point apps/api/.env's DATABASE_URL at prod, then npm run api:dev and npm run web:dev. Your local code has the segment filters, so you'll see it exactly as it'll look post-merge.
7. Put the local .env files back when you're done, so you don't later run tests or prisma:seed against prod.
If you want to undo the ingestion
This is what makes step 2 more than paranoia — the data side is cleanly reversible without the backup:
DELETE FROM "PlayerGameStat" WHERE "gameId" IN (SELECT id FROM "Game" WHERE "seasonType" <> 'REGULAR');
DELETE FROM "GameEvent"      WHERE "gameId" IN (SELECT id FROM "Game" WHERE "seasonType" <> 'REGULAR');
DELETE FROM "Game" WHERE "seasonType" <> 'REGULAR';
The migration itself doesn't need reverting — two nullable/defaulted columns that no deployed code reads yet.
The one thing to never do while .env points at prod: npm run prisma:seed. resetGameData() deletes every Game, GameEvent and PlayerGameStat row unconditionally. That's the real hazard in this whole sequence, and it's one command away from what you've been running locally all day.

?sslmode=require. What does appending this to the database url do?

Assistant
2026/09/07, 15:19:33
[ { "type": "thinking", "thinking": "", "signature": "" } ]

Assistant
2026/09/07, 15:19:43
It's a libpq connection parameter, not something Prisma or Python invented — it's part of the standard PostgreSQL connection string, and both psycopg2 (your ingestion) and Prisma pass it through.
sslmode=require tells the client: encrypt this connection with TLS, and fail if you can't.
You need it because the External Database URL goes over the public internet, and Render's managed Postgres refuses unencrypted external connections. Without it you're sending your database credentials and every row in transit across the open internet.
The important caveat
require is weaker than it sounds. The full ladder:
Mode	Encrypts	Verifies cert chain	Verifies hostname
disable	no	—	—
prefer (libpq default)	if offered, else silently plaintext	no	no
require	yes	no	no
verify-ca	yes	yes	no
verify-full	yes	yes	yes

So require stops passive eavesdropping but not an active man-in-the-middle — it encrypts to whoever answers, without checking that whoever answered is really Render. verify-full is the one that's actually secure end to end; it needs the CA cert available to the client, which is why require is the common pragmatic default for one-off admin connections like this.
For a one-off ingestion run from your own machine, require is a reasonable call. It'd be the wrong default for something long-lived.
Two practical notes
Render's URL usually already includes it. Check before appending — you don't want ...?sslmode=require?sslmode=require. Query strings take ? for the first parameter and & for every one after, so if the URL already has any parameter, yours needs &sslmode=require.
Omitting it fails loudly, not silently. The libpq default is prefer, which falls back to plaintext if the server allows it. Render doesn't allow it, so you'd get a connection error rather than an unnoticed unencrypted connection. That's the good outcome — but don't rely on it as your security model.
Your local .env correctly has no sslmode: localhost:55432 never leaves the machine, and the docker-compose Postgres isn't configured for TLS anyway, so adding require there would just break the connection.

The rule catches your backup and leaves Prisma migrations tracked.
To summarise
What went wrong: pg_dump only dumps backwards — a 16.x client refuses a 17.x server, by design, because it can't know how to serialise catalog structures introduced after it was built. The reverse (17 dumping a 16 server) is fine. Your local compose file pins postgres:16-alpine, but Render provisioned 17.6.
The fix:
docker run --rm postgres:17-alpine pg_dump "<PROD_URL>" > prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql
Then confirm it's real before trusting it as a backup — a failed dump leaves a plausible-looking file:
Get-Item prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql | Select-Object Length
Select-String -Path prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql -Pattern "PostgreSQL database dump complete" 
That trailing marker is the last line pg_dump writes, so its presence is your proof the dump finished rather than died partway.
Worth keeping in mind that the same version rule will apply if you ever restore: use a 17 client, and note your local docker-compose Postgres is 16, so this dump won't restore into your local dev DB without bumping that image.
The .gitignore change is uncommitted, alongside ingest_postseason.py and its README section. I'd suggest committing the ignore rule on its own as chore: ignore database dumps — it's an unrelated safety fix, not part of the postseason feature. Assistant
2026/09/07, 16:08:37
Verified — clean UTF-8 (2d 2d 0a = --\n, no BOM, no null bytes), and the completion marker is present.
What went wrong
Nothing was hanging, and the dump wasn't failing. pg_dump writes to stdout, which you redirected — so silence in the terminal is exactly what success looks like. It had already written 10.4 MB at 16:04.
The actual bug is subtler: Windows PowerShell 5.1's > operator re-encodes as UTF-16LE. So you got a complete, valid dump that psql cannot restore, at double the size. That's the worst failure mode for a backup — it looks fine until the day you need it.
The fix: let pg_dump write the file itself
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/backup" postgres:17-alpine pg_dump "<PROD_URL>" -n public --no-owner --no-acl -f /backup/prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql
The volume mount plus -f keeps PowerShell out of the data path entirely, so nothing re-encodes it.
Two flags worth having, given prod is Supabase:
    • -n public limits the dump to your app's schema. Your current dump carries Supabase's auth.users, auth.refresh_tokens and auth.identities — live credentials you don't need for a postseason rollback, and shouldn't have sitting in your project folder. It also halves the size.
    • --no-owner --no-acl drops role grants that won't exist wherever you restore, which is what usually makes a Supabase dump fail to replay.
Then verify it's genuinely complete:
Select-String -Path prod-backup-2026-09-07.sql -Pattern "PostgreSQL database dump complete"
One match means pg_dump reached the end. No match means it died partway, regardless of file size.
The existing UTF-16 file will just be overwritten. It's covered by the .gitignore rule, so it was never at risk of being committed.
Note for the ingestion step: you're running these commands in PowerShell, so /backup passes through fine. That Git Bash path-mangling error above was my shell, not yours — but if you ever switch to Git Bash for a docker run -v, prefix it with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1.

Both work. Here's the corrected command:
docker run --rm postgres:17-alpine psql "<PROD_URL>" -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM \"Team\";'
Single quotes outside, \" inside. Counter-intuitively you need the backslashes inside single quotes — PowerShell passes \" through literally, and the executable's C runtime unescapes it into a real ". Verified against your local DB: returns 4.
Why my version failed: I've been running these through the Bash tool, where \" inside double quotes works fine. PowerShell 5.1 strips embedded double quotes when building native-command argument lists, so the same string arrives mangled. My mistake for handing you a bash-shaped command.
Also worth knowing: plain single quotes with bare "Team" inside also fails — PowerShell eats those quotes too, leaving FROM Team, which Postgres folds to lowercase team and can't find. The backslashes aren't optional.
For the multi-statement rollback SQL
The same problem would hit the DELETE statements I gave you earlier, and getting quoting wrong on a DELETE against prod is a much worse day than getting it wrong on a SELECT. Put them in a file instead and skip shell quoting entirely:
# save as rollback-postseason.sql (it's covered by the *-backup-*.sql ignore only if named that way,
# so keep it out of the repo or name it accordingly)
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/sql" postgres:17-alpine psql "<PROD_URL>" -f /sql/rollback-postseason.sql
One caution on a tempting shortcut
pg_stat_user_tables.n_live_tup avoids quoting altogether, but don't use it to check row counts — in my test it reported 0 for every table on a database that definitely has rows, because it's a planner estimate that's only refreshed by ANALYZE/autovacuum. Use count(*) and pay the quoting tax.

Good news and a fork in the road.
Verified: my derivations match NBA's official numbers exactly (all three columns agree to 3 decimals across a real Finals boxscore). So these three need no schema change and no re-ingestion — they work retroactively on every row you already have, postseason included:
Stat	Formula	Status
eFG%	(FGM + 0.5·3PM) / FGA	✅ derive at request time
TS%	PTS / (2·(FGA + 0.44·FTA))	✅ derive at request time
AST:TO	AST / TOV	✅ derive at request time

That also matches the codebase's existing philosophy — stats.service.ts already computes FG% from summed makes/attempts rather than storing it.
The other four can't be honestly derived from what we store:
    • +/- is a raw observation, not a calculation. Good news: it's already in the BoxScoreTraditionalV3 response we fetch — we just throw it away. So it costs zero extra API calls, only a column and a re-ingest.
    • Usage%, ORtg, DRtg need BoxScoreAdvancedV3 — a second call per game. Oliver's individual ratings need possession estimates and opponent context we simply don't have. Computing them from our columns would be fabricating a statistic, which is exactly what four_factors.py refused to do for offensive rebound rate.
Taking that dependency roughly doubles the boxscore call budget (~540 extra calls, +9–10 min), and those four columns stay null for all existing prod data until a full re-ingest — not just the postseason script.
Bonus finding: the same response also carries reboundsOffensive/reboundsDefensive, which is the exact data four_factors.py documents as missing — it left offensive rebound rate out of the Four Factors for want of it. Storing it would unblock that model too.
This directly affects the prod run you're mid-way through, so it's worth deciding before you ingest.

Complete: 110 API tests, 160 web, 18 ingestion. All seven stats delivered.
Where	What you get
Profile — per-game tiles	USG%, +/-, ORTG, DRTG added. Widened to 6 columns so all 12 tiles form two clean rows instead of a ragged trailing one.
Profile — shooting splits	TS% and eFG% joined FG%/3P%/FT%/FTA-G, all six on one line.
Splits table	Seven new rows, ordered production → shooting → efficiency → impact.
Compare	New "Other" section: TS%, eFG%, Usage%, AST:TO, +/-, ORtg, DRtg.

Three judgement calls worth your review:
    • The advanced tiles aren't editable. The local "what if" overlay lets you explore how a player's own production would change, but usage and the ratings are measured against teammates and opponents — a hand-typed value wouldn't mean anything. TS%/eFG% are excluded for a different reason: they're derived from the makes/attempts shown beside them, so an editable TS% could contradict an unchanged FG%.
    • Defensive rating inverts the colour coding. It's points conceded per 100 possessions, so a fall is an improvement. Without that, a playoff defensive improvement would have been painted red. Same inversion applied to the compare page's "best" highlight.
    • Nulls render as "—", never 0. A zero plus/minus is an even game and 0% usage means never touching the ball — both real measurements. Existing prod rows will show "—" for the four stored stats until the re-ingest.
Proposed commits:

1	feat: store plus-minus, usage and player ratings per game (schema, migration, ingestion, seed)
2	feat: derive true shooting, effective FG% and assist-to-turnover (stats service + specs)
3	feat: show advanced stats on profile, splits and comparison pages (web)
4	docs: document the advanced stats and their sources
5	chore: ignore database dumps (the .gitignore safety fix, carried over)

What it will do
The full ingest.py refreshes teams, rosters, bios, regular-season games and the postseason, filling the six new columns across all 33,662 stat rows. Every write is an upsert keyed on real NBA ids, so nothing is deleted or duplicated — existing rows get updated in place.
~40–50 minutes, roughly 1,500–1,700 calls. It must run from your residential connection.
Steps
1. Confirm .env still points at prod (it did last I checked, but verify rather than assume — that's the mistake I made):
Select-String -Path apps\ingestion\.env -Pattern "supabase"
2. Take a fresh backup first. Your existing one is the UTF-16 file, which won't restore:
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/backup" postgres:17-alpine pg_dump "<PROD_URL>" -n public --no-owner --no-acl -f /backup/prod-backup-pre-reingest.sql
Select-String -Path prod-backup-pre-reingest.sql -Pattern "PostgreSQL database dump complete"
One match means it finished. That file is covered by the .gitignore rule I just committed.
3. Run it. Use Tee-Object so you keep the log — with ~1,500 calls, you want a record of any game that failed:
cd apps\ingestion
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe ingest.py 2>&1 | Tee-Object -FilePath ingest-log.txt
Watch for Advanced boxscore unavailable for game …. Those games keep their traditional stats and get null advanced ones — re-running fills them in, since the upsert uses COALESCE and won't null out what's already there.
Verifying it worked
docker run --rm postgres:17-alpine psql "<PROD_URL>" -c 'SELECT count(*) AS total, count(\"plusMinus\") AS with_plusminus, count(\"usagePercentage\") AS with_usage FROM \"PlayerGameStat\";'
All three numbers should be close to equal. A large gap between total and with_usage means advanced calls were failing — check the log and re-run.
Then spot-check a real player against NBA.com. Their season TS%/eFG% should match exactly; usage and the ratings are NBA's own figures, though our minutes-weighted season aggregate may differ slightly from NBA.com's own season-level calculation, which derives from season totals rather than averaging per-game figures. Per-game values will match precisely.
Two cautions
    • Never npm run prisma:seed while .env points at prod. resetGameData() deletes every Game, GameEvent and PlayerGameStat row unconditionally. It's still the sharpest edge in this whole sequence.
    • Point both .env files back at localhost when you're done, so a later test run or seed can't reach prod.
One thing worth weighing: running this before review means prod carries data the deployed code can't display yet. That's harmless — the extra columns are simply unread — but if you'd rather keep prod and main in lockstep, merging both branches first costs you nothing except the wait.

Answering this properly turned up three things, including that my instructions were wrong.
Why a re-ingest is needed at all
Only for four of the seven stats. The split matters:
    • TS%, eFG%, AST:TO are derived from columns you already have. They work on all 33,662 existing rows right now, no ingestion required.
    • Plus/minus, Usage%, ORtg, DRtg are stored. They can't be computed from what we hold — plus/minus is an observation, and individual ratings need possession and opponent context the schema doesn't carry. The columns exist but are null on 33,636 rows. Only fetching from the API fills them.
So the re-ingest buys you exactly those four.
Why "run ingest.py" was the wrong instruction
Two problems, and the first is serious:
It would only cover a third of your games. fetch_recent_games is capped at GAMES_PER_TEAM = 15, so a run touches roughly 400 unique games. Prod has 1,242 regular-season games spanning October to April, accumulated over many runs. The other ~840 would keep null advanced stats permanently. My verification step ("counts should be close to equal") would have failed and I'd have told you to re-run something that structurally cannot finish the job.
It also wastes ~500 calls re-fetching player bios that are already correct.
The much better option
PlayerGameLogs returns 26,651 player-game rows in a single call — the whole season, with PLUS_MINUS/OREB/DREB in the base measure and USG_PCT/OFF_RATING/DEF_RATING in the advanced one. Keyed by GAME_ID and PLAYER_ID, which map straight onto our nbaGameId/nbaPlayerId.
I verified coverage: 1,230 of 1,230 real games, 100%.
That makes the backfill roughly 8 calls and a few seconds, instead of 2,666 calls and 45 minutes.
Two things this surfaced
Prod contains 12 mock games. The dozen "uncovered" games were MOCK-GAME-0 … MOCK-GAME-11, dated Oct–Nov 2025 — prisma:seed fixtures with randomly generated boxscores, sitting in production and being served as real data. They're the reason your regular-season count is 1,242 rather than 1,230.
The design I just committed is probably wrong. I built ingestion around a per-game BoxScoreAdvancedV3 call, doubling the ongoing call budget by ~900 calls per run. PlayerGameLogs would do the same job in ~4 calls. I should have looked for a bulk endpoint before committing to the per-game one.

Both discrepancies explained, and confirmed the mock deletion worked (0 remaining).
The 33,590 vs 28,698 gap
It cuts both ways:
5,806 stored rows have no feed row. BoxScoreTraditionalV3 includes every player on the roster, including those who didn't play — 0 minutes, all zeros. PlayerGameLogs only lists players who actually appeared. Those DNPs correctly stay null: a player who didn't play has no usage rate.
~914 feed rows have no stored row. The feed covers the whole league; we only store players on ingested rosters, so two-way and call-up players who appear in a boxscore get skipped (existing behaviour, documented in ingest.py).
Net: 33,590 − 5,806 DNPs = 27,784 played, and about 28,017 will match. That small overshoot is a nice detail — _parse_minutes_to_int floors "0:35" to 0 minutes, so a few hundred players who played under a minute are stored as DNPs but do appear in the feed. They'll get backfilled correctly.
The speed — that one's on me
I said "seconds, not 45 minutes." That was about the API calls, and it's true: 6 calls, done in the first few seconds, as your output shows.
But the script then does 28,017 individual UPDATE statements, one network round trip each, against the Supabase pooler. At ~40ms per round trip that's roughly 20 minutes. I framed the whole operation by its cheapest part.
Let it finish — it's correct and idempotent, and it's already 2,524 rows in. Interrupting buys nothing; a re-run would just redo the same work.
For future runs the fix is straightforward: batch the updates with psycopg2.extras.execute_batch or a single UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...), which would genuinely make it seconds. Same pattern game-detail.service.ts already uses on the API side — the codebase has a documented history of exactly this N+1 mistake against a network-hop database, and I walked into it again.
Want me to write that batching fix now so it's ready for the next run, or leave the script as-is since it's a one-off?

Verified — yes, it's safe. Three things confirm it:
1. Every call site is throttled. I audited all of them; player_game_logs.py:116 wraps PlayerGameLogs in call_with_rate_limit, same as every other endpoint in the pipeline. Nothing bypasses it.
2. The backfill makes 6 API calls, total. Your output shows all of them already completed in the first few seconds:
Fetched 26651 Regular Season player-game rows.   ← 2 calls (Base + Advanced)
Fetched 126 PlayIn player-game rows.             ← 2 calls
Fetched 1921 Playoffs player-game rows.          ← 2 calls
Everything since — the Backfilled 500…1000… lines — is pure database writes. There is zero stats.nba.com traffic in the part you're watching. The rate limiter is irrelevant to it.
3. The refactor reduced exposure rather than increasing it. The per-game BoxScoreAdvancedV3 design I replaced would have made ~900 calls to fetch the same figures. Six calls is roughly 150× less traffic, so if anything this is gentler on the endpoint than what's already in main.
RATE_LIMIT_DELAY_SECONDS = 1.0 sleeps before each call, so there's no opening burst, and the 3-attempt retry with 3-second backoff still applies.
One honest caveat. The trade is fewer, larger requests: a 26,651-row response is a much bigger payload than a single boxscore, which is why I gave it timeout=60 rather than the 30 used elsewhere. Fewer requests is the safer direction for rate limiting, but a large response has more room to time out on a flaky connection. It succeeded cleanly on both my verification runs and yours, so it's empirically fine — and if it ever did fail, the retry handles it and the script is idempotent.
The thing genuinely worth watching in this script is the ~20 minutes of row-by-row UPDATEs against Supabase, which is a database-load question, not a rate-limit one. It's light work per row and safely batched at every 500 commits.

Computing those locally would be inventing a statistic, which is the same call four_factors.py already makes about Oliver's offensive-rebound factor.\n\n## Nulls are meaningful\n\nEvery stored figure is nullable, and every aggregate returns null rather than 0 when no game carries it. A zero plus/minus is an even game; a 0% usage rate is a player who never touched the ball. Both are real measurements, so "not recorded" has to stay distinguishable. The UI renders null as "—" throughout, and a delta is only drawn when both ends exist — comparing against a missing baseline would treat "not recorded" as zero and invent a change that never happened.\n\n## Two details worth a second opinion\n\nDefensive rating inverts. It's points conceded per 100 possessions, so a fall is an improvement. Both the splits table's colour coding and the compare page's "best" highlight invert for it. Without that, a playoff defensive improvement would render red and lose the comparison.\n\nUsage and the ratings are minutes-weighted, not plain means. They're rates over playing time, so a four-minute garbage-time cameo shouldn't count as much as a 38-minute start. This means our season figure may differ slightly from NBA.com's own season-level calculation, which derives from season totals. Per-game values match exactly.\n\n## The advanced tiles aren't editable\n\nThe profile's local "what if" overlay stays limited to counting stats. Usage and the ratings are measured against teammates and opponents, so a hand-typed value wouldn't mean anything. TS%/eFG% are excluded for a different reason: they're derived from the makes and attempts shown beside them, so an editable TS% could contradict an unchanged FG%.\n\n## Ingestion: 6 calls, not ~900\n\n48efd83 replaces a per-game BoxScoreAdvancedV3 call with leaguewide PlayerGameLogs, which returns every player-game row for a whole segment in one call (26,651 for the 2025-26 regular season). Two measure types per segment covers everything, so a full season including postseason costs 6 calls instead of roughly 900 — the difference between adding ~15 minutes to every ingestion run and adding about six seconds.\n\nI committed the per-game version first and replaced it once I found the bulk endpoint; the refactor is kept as its own commit rather than squashed, so the reasoning is visible.\n\n## Production is already backfilled\n\nbackfill_advanced_stats.py has already been run against prod. main has moved since you branched, and it contains three CI fixes your branches don't have:
4d32d4f  fix: enhance Postgres reachability checks in CI by using job-specific network
cb3d9dc  fix: improve Postgres container startup and reachability checks in CI

Your branch is running the old ci.yml, where the coverage job couldn't reach its Postgres container. That's why it fails in 15 seconds — far too fast to be a test failure — while lint and typecheck, which need no database, pass fine.
That's exactly what Gitea's "This branch is out-of-date with the base branch" warning is pointing at. Clicking Update branch by merge (or git merge origin/main locally) pulls in the fix. The check should go green with no code change.

Why merge main in
Your branches were cut from an older main. Since then it's gained 5 commits, three of which fix the CI workflow:
6f76c82  fix: update CI configuration for concurrency and Postgres setup
cb3d9dc  fix: improve Postgres container startup and reachability checks
4d32d4f  fix: enhance Postgres reachability checks by using job-specific network
Your branch still runs the old .gitea/workflows/ci.yml, where the coverage job couldn't reach its Postgres container. That's your red check — failing in 15 seconds, far too fast to be a test failure, while lint and typecheck (which need no database) pass fine. Someone else hit this and fixed it on main; you just don't have the fix yet.
So merging main isn't housekeeping — it's the actual fix for the failing check. Nothing in your code is wrong.
The other two commits are the home-page PR (#87), which you'd inherit anyway on merge.
I also checked: zero conflicts. The merge is clean.
No, you don't need new PRs
A PR tracks a branch, not a snapshot. Anything you push to postseason-view — the navigation fix, the merge commit, both — updates PR #89 in place and re-triggers CI. Same for PR 2. Your existing PRs, review comments and discussion all stay.
That's precisely what Gitea's "Update branch by merge" button does: it creates a merge commit on your branch and pushes it. Doing it locally with git merge origin/main is the same operation, just with visibility if something did conflict.
Either route works here. The button is fine given there are no conflicts — the only advantage of doing it locally is that I can run the tests afterwards to confirm the merged result is green before you push.
One thing to note
I'd merge rather than rebase. Both branches are already pushed with PRs open and a teammate has reviewed them; rebasing would rewrite commits they've already read and force-push over the history their comments are anchored to.
Order matters for the stack: main → postseason-view, then postseason-view → advanced-player-stats, so PR 2 doesn't show PR 1's changes twice.
